title: Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy-Related Inflammation: Report of a Case with Very Difficult Therapeutic Management
case_prompt: An 81-year-old man was admitted with sudden onset of left hemiparesis and delirium. On examination, he had left homonymous hemianopia, dysarthria, spatial and temporal disorientation, sensory aphasia, and psychomotor slowing. Vital signs were stable. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 66 mm/h, with otherwise unremarkable blood tests. A CT scan showed left occipital hypodensity, a right middle cerebral artery–territory hypodensity with hyperdense foci, and right lateral ventricular compression. EEG demonstrated subcontinuous 1–2 Hz delta waves and sharp waves predominantly on the right. Brain MRI revealed large asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter lesions in the right hemisphere and left occipital lobe, consistent with vasogenic edema. GRE sequences showed multiple cortical and subcortical microhemorrhages in the temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes bilaterally (more extensive on the right). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis disclosed mildly elevated protein and cell count but no evidence of infection.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) was considered but “excluded because of patient's age and clinical presentation, together with lack of predisposing conditions.”  
2. Noninflammatory cerebral amyloid angiopathy was considered but “patients with PRES and those with noninflammatory CAA have symmetric lesions, whereas patients with CAA-ri have asymmetric inflammatory lesions, as in our patient.”  
3. Mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like syndrome (MELAS) was considered but “excluded because of clinical presentation and age of the patient.”  
4. Meningoencephalitis was considered but “the patient's clinical presentation, blood examinations, and lumbar puncture allowed us to exclude meningoencephalitis.”  
5. Vasculitis was considered but “the patient's clinical presentation, blood examinations, and lumbar puncture allowed us to exclude … vasculitis.”  
6. Support for CAA-ri included “the response to steroid therapy and the demonstration of the APO-E ε4/ε4 genotype helped to clarify the diagnosis,” and elevated CSF anti–beta amyloid autoantibodies further supported an autoimmune reaction to β-amyloid deposits.
